panel.name: Synthetic 01 — Constitutional lawyer
panel.text: Citizens’ assemblies should advise Parliament, not make binding law. Random selection can broaden whose views are heard, but a small panel cannot inherit the mandate of an election. Stratified recruitment is appropriate if its limits are published. Parliament should publish a reasoned response within six months, while retaining the right to reject recommendations. Pay participants and cover caring costs so participation is possible for people without spare income.

panel.name: Synthetic 02 — Community organiser
panel.text: Advice alone is too easy for ministers to ignore. A citizens’ assembly should be able to trigger a parliamentary debate, although it should not legislate directly. A reasoned government response within six months would be a minimum safeguard. Recruitment must actively reach people who distrust institutions; a mailed lottery by itself will miss them. Pay for time, childcare and interpreters, and allow community groups to challenge gaps in the panel.

panel.name: Synthetic 03 — Sampling statistician
panel.text: Use a stratified civic lottery, publish recruitment and dropout rates, and report uncertainty rather than claiming a miniature nation has spoken. I cannot judge whether six months is the right response deadline without evidence about the workload. Paying participants is essential to reduce selection bias, but money alone does not solve nonresponse. Recommendations should remain advisory. The public should see the minority reasons as well as the final vote totals.

panel.name: Synthetic 04 — Disability access researcher
panel.text: An assembly is not representative if disabled citizens cannot participate in its meetings. Fund accessible venues, personal assistance, transport, communication support and caring costs, alongside payment for time. Hybrid attendance should be an option, never the only route. I support a guaranteed parliamentary debate, but I am undecided about binding powers because process accessibility does not by itself establish democratic authority. Publish accessibility outcomes and provide an independent complaints route.

panel.name: Synthetic 05 — Local government practitioner
panel.text: Start with local planning and service trade-offs where participants can see the consequences of their advice. Councils should publish a response within six months, but a mandatory Westminster debate for every local assembly would be disproportionate. Recommendations should be advisory, with elected councillors responsible for budgets. Pay expenses and a modest attendance allowance. Recruitment should combine a civic lottery with targeted follow-up to fill missing neighbourhood and age groups.

panel.name: Synthetic 06 — Public finance analyst
panel.text: I am not convinced that every participant should receive an attendance payment in addition to expenses; test whether targeted income replacement improves inclusion at reasonable cost. Assemblies should remain advisory and should not compel a parliamentary debate. A six-month reasoned response is a practical accountability rule. Publish the full cost per participant, alternative consultation costs and independent evaluations before creating a permanent national programme.

panel.name: Synthetic 07 — Climate policy campaigner
panel.text: Climate assemblies need more influence than optional advice. A sufficiently supported recommendation should trigger a parliamentary debate and a public response within six months. I would consider binding authority over a limited, pre-agreed local spending pot, but not a power to rewrite national law. Pay all participants and their access costs. Provide balanced evidence without pretending that unsupported scientific claims deserve equal weight, and publish dissenting reasons.

panel.name: Synthetic 08 — Rural services advocate
panel.text: A national panel can overlook distance, unreliable transport and seasonal work. Stratify recruitment by geography and deprivation, cover travel and replacement caring costs, and pay for participants’ time. Keep recommendations advisory; a compulsory parliamentary debate may reward headline topics over rural priorities. I am unsure whether six months is feasible for every proposal. Require a public timetable instead, with explanations when ministers need longer.

panel.name: Synthetic 09 — Small business representative
panel.text: Assemblies should advise elected decision-makers, not exercise binding powers or automatically command parliamentary time. Participants need access to evidence about jobs, tax and implementation costs as well as campaign arguments. I support a six-month written response and targeted compensation for lost earnings rather than an identical payment to everyone. Publish recruitment methods and conflicts of interest so organised interests cannot dominate the discussion.

panel.name: Synthetic 10 — Parliamentary scrutiny researcher
panel.text: An assembly should have the right to a committee hearing rather than automatically triggering a full parliamentary debate. Its recommendations should remain advisory, with a reasoned government response within six months and explicit explanations for rejection. A stratified lottery, published evidence and minority reports would make scrutiny more credible. Pay participants and cover access needs. After an initial pilot, evaluate whether recommendations actually improve decisions before expanding the programme.

audited_claims.title: Citizens’ assemblies should remain advisory rather than have binding powers.
Citizens’ assemblies should trigger a guaranteed parliamentary debate.
Elected bodies should publish a reasoned response within six months.
All participants should receive payment for their time.

status: Round one: ten responses, audited synthesis saved as v4. Round two: one completed response and one partial draft. Round three: empty, became active unexpectedly; restoration pending make_active endpoint compatibility fix. Remaining nineteen synthetic submissions require exact-batch confirmation after automatic approval review rejection.

comments: Parliament must retain final responsibility for law; an assembly can strengthen scrutiny without replacing elected consent.
A guaranteed committee hearing may be sufficient; I am neutral on requiring a full chamber debate.
A reasoned response within six months creates an accountable obligation without compelling acceptance.
Payment removes a financial barrier; caring expenses should be funded separately.
Advisory recommendations can still have influence if elected representatives must answer publicly.
Without protected parliamentary time, communities may see the exercise as consultation without consequences.
Six months is already a long wait for communities asked to volunteer substantial time.
A universal attendance payment avoids making lower-income participants prove financial hardship.
Sampling cannot confer the same mandate as a national election, so recommendations should remain advisory.
I need evidence about parliamentary capacity and how a debate threshold would be chosen.
No workload estimates have been supplied; I still cannot assess whether six months is feasible.
Payment helps reduce nonresponse bias, although recruitment quality also matters.
ratings: Unable to judge — need more information
Unable to judge — need more information

comments: I have not resolved whether a fully accessible process could justify limited binding powers.
A guaranteed debate would give excluded participants confidence that their work will be heard.
The response should be available in accessible formats within the same six-month deadline.
Disabled participants need payment for their time plus separate access support; one cannot replace the other.
ratings: Unable to judge — need more information

comments: Councillors must remain accountable for local budgets and implementation.
Not every local recommendation merits a Westminster debate; local scrutiny should be the normal route.
Councils can explain acceptance, rejection or outstanding work within six months.
A modest attendance allowance recognises time without making participation a source of profit.
Binding commitments could create expenditure outside the elected budget process.
Compulsory debates have an opportunity cost and should not follow every recommendation automatically.
A written response is a relatively low-cost accountability mechanism.
I prefer income replacement targeted at those facing losses rather than identical payments to everyone.
A limited local spending pot could be delegated in advance; this claim rules that possibility out too broadly.
A sufficiently supported recommendation needs a guaranteed route onto the political agenda.
Urgent climate proposals should not disappear into an indefinite review process.
Universal payment lets people without spare income participate in demanding deliberation.
Elected representatives must weigh recommendations against less visible rural priorities.
Automatic debates may favour high-profile campaigns while rural needs receive little attention.
Complex rural transport proposals may take longer to assess; I need clarity about what a response must contain.
Travel and replacement care must be covered in addition to time spent in meetings.
ratings: Unable to judge — need more information

comments: Business regulation requires elected accountability and clarity over who makes the final decision.
An automatic claim on parliamentary time could encourage organised lobbying through assembly recommendations.
A written explanation within six months would help organisations plan around unresolved proposals.
Targeted lost-income support would be a better use of funds than paying people who incur no loss.
Advisory assemblies can complement scrutiny without creating a competing mandate.
A committee hearing provides examination and a public record without requiring a full debate.
Rejection should receive as much explanation as acceptance within the response period.
Payment recognises deliberative work and should be transparent and consistent.
I retain strong support: the discussion reinforces the need for a clear line of elected accountability.
I remain neutral between a committee hearing and a full debate; scrutiny quality matters more than the venue.
I support the deadline provided the explanation distinguishes a decision from work still under assessment.
The discussion has not altered my support for paying time and reimbursing care separately.
The panel has clarified that advisory status need not mean recommendations can be ignored.
I still support a guaranteed debate, but the rural and scrutiny concerns make me favour a meaningful threshold.
A public six-month response remains the minimum commitment I would ask communities to accept.
I retain strong support for a basic payment that does not require a means test.
No argument in the feedback gives a sampled panel an electoral mandate to make binding national law.
The panel offers competing institutional arguments, but insufficient evidence to choose a mandatory debate rule.
An interim-response proposal helps, but I still lack information about workloads and enforceability.
Recruitment bias remains my principal reason for strongly supporting payment.
ratings: Unable to judge — need more information
Unable to judge — need more information

comments: The distinction between accessible participation and final elected authority persuades me to support advisory powers.
I continue to support a debate, with an accessible public record of how recommendations were considered.
I support a reasoned response that is accessible to the people who took part, not only a published PDF.
Strong support remains: access budgets should not be deducted from the attendance payment.
I still support retaining elected responsibility for decisions made with local public funds.
The debate threshold suggestion does not resolve my concern about treating local assemblies as national issues.
A response can explain unresolved feasibility work without promising delivery within six months.
A modest allowance plus expenses remains proportionate for a local assembly.
I retain strong support for an advisory role because budget responsibility cannot be dispersed without safeguards.
I still oppose an automatic debate entitlement; a committee can decide where parliamentary time adds value.
The distinction between a reasoned response and implementation makes the deadline workable in principle.
I move to neutral: a modest universal allowance combined with targeted lost-income support may balance cost and access.
I remain opposed to the blanket wording; a pre-authorised local budget is a defensible exception.
A guaranteed debate remains essential to prevent ambitious recommendations from being quietly shelved.
I strongly support the deadline, including reasons when a proposal is rejected.
The finance objections do not outweigh the inclusion case for a basic payment to everyone.
Advisory status lets elected bodies compare an assembly proposal with other underserved places.
A threshold could still favour organised urban campaigns, so I continue to oppose an automatic debate.
I now agree because a reasoned interim response can explain remaining work without promising an immediate final decision.
I retain strong support: geography creates time costs as well as travel expenses.
Final authority should remain with elected decision-makers who can be held accountable for regulation.
I still prefer a scrutiny route that can assess lobbying risk before allocating a full debate.
The clarified deadline gives a useful planning signal even where a final decision is not possible.
I continue to prefer targeted compensation; the panel has not demonstrated the additional value of universal payments.
The discussion supports an advisory contribution embedded in existing scrutiny institutions.
I remain against a guaranteed full debate; a committee hearing is a more proportionate default.
A response should identify who owns any outstanding work and state when it will return for scrutiny.
I continue to support transparent payment rules and separate access funding.
